sources: Time-of-check to time-of-use race, check and write separated by a lock release (CWE-367)
Lock-order inversion between two locks taken in opposite orders (CWE-833)
Retention deleting work that is still pending (spec R3 in spec.md)

defects.class: check-then-act race: version checked under one lock acquisition, written under another without re-check
defects.description: Line 53 (if version <= current) runs under the plan lock, which is released at line 55 before the patch is built (line 56). The write at line 59 re-acquires plan then store and does not re-check the applied version. Failing input: apply(P, v2) and apply(P, v3) with applied version 1. Both pass the check at line 53. v2 blocks while building its patch; v3 completes and writes applied v3; then v2 writes at line 59 and overwrites it. Final applied_version(P) = 2 and applied_payload(P) = {dose: 2}, while spec R2 requires v3 to remain. Control run on base/ (check and write in one plan-lock section) ends at applied_version 3, payload {dose: 3}. Correction from audit: the plan lock is released after line 52; the check is at line 53; the write at line 59 does not re-check.

evidence.interleaving: scripted with threading.Event: v2 is held inside _build_patch after its check; v3 runs to completion; v2 then writes

defects.class: retention removes pending rows that the spec protects
defects.description: delete_older_than deletes every row whose store-wide seq is below the horizon, regardless of status. The horizon comes from cleaner.py sweep_once (cleaner.py lines 50-51), which uses the latest applied seq across all plan ids. Failing input: put_pending(B, v1) gets seq 1; put_pending(A, v1) gets seq 2; apply(A, v1) writes an applied row with seq 3. sweep_once then computes horizon 3 and deletes seq 1 and seq 2, so the pending B row is gone. apply_next(B) returns nothing_pending and applied_version(B) stays 0. Expected: B v1 applied (spec R3 and R5 violated). The same result occurs on base/ with the same method, so the flaw is in code this change did not touch; the new cleaner thread makes it reachable.

code_output: pending row for B after sweep: None
base_control_output: pending row for B after sweep: None

defects.description: sweep_once takes the store lock (line 50) and then requests the plan lock (line 52). locks.py (lines 1-8) documents the order plan before store, and applier.py takes plan (line 57) then store (line 58). Failing input: one thread runs sweep_once while another runs apply(P, v1). The cleaner holds store and waits for plan; the applier holds plan and waits for store. Both threads block indefinitely. Scripted run with gates that place each thread between its first and second acquisition: both threads still alive after 3 s joins. Spec R4 violated.

code_output: DEADLOCK: cleaner waits on plan (held by applier); applier waits on store (held by cleaner)
evidence.interleaving: gates: applier waits for cleaner to hold store before its check; cleaner waits for applier to hold plan before taking plan; applier signals before taking store

decoys.why_not_a_defect: VersionCounter.next is a read-modify-write (get, add 1, store) inside its own lock: with self._lock. Under concurrent calls each caller gets a distinct value. Checked: three calls return [1, 2, 3]. Same read-then-write shape as D1, but the whole sequence is under one lock acquisition.

save_snapshot writes to a temp file created in the same directory, fsyncs it, then calls os.replace, which is atomic on the same filesystem. Checked: a 1-row store writes a snapshot with 1 row and leaves no .tmp file behind. Looks like an unsafe in-place overwrite but is not.

queue.Queue is consumed only by the single thread started in start(), through _run. Two request_sweep calls followed by stop produce exactly 2 sweeps (checked). Multiple producers are safe with queue.Queue; there is one consumer, so no concurrent get.

The write block takes the plan lock (line 57) and then the store lock (line 58), which is the order documented in locks.py. Same nested-acquisition syntax as the defect in cleaner.py, but correct here. Base control run with this order ends at applied_version 3 for the v2/v3 interleaving, as spec R2 requires.

Real flaw, unchanged line: put_pending stores the caller's payload dict by reference. Checked: after d = {dose: 5}; put_pending(C, 1, d); d[dose] = 50, pending_row(C).payload is {dose: 50}. Pre-existing and outside the diff; a diff-mode reviewer must not report it as a defect of this change.

accepted_extras.description: save_snapshot: on a serialisation error the mkstemp fd stays open and cleanup can raise, masking the original error and leaving a tmp file (latent, outside the diff).
